summary: A 1970 note commenting on the network protocol discussed in RFC 36. It is one of several responses from sites in the group on the proposals for the host-to-host protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 38 comments on the host-to-host protocol proposed in RFC 36. It argues that a link should be able to carry more than one connection and suggests adding socket information to messages.

questions: how could connections share an arpanet link
subtitle: A comment proposing that several connections share one ARPANET link.

tldr.problem: RFC 36's proposed protocol did not allow several connections to be multiplexed over one link.
tldr.mechanism: Stephen Wolfe suggests identifying sockets in control messages and adding the destination socket to each data-message header, while leaving multiplexing itself optional for the time being.
tldr.outcome: RFC 38 is an early protocol-design comment on RFC 36; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

today: RFC 38 is an early comment on RFC 36. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: Why Share a Link
sections.content:
Stephen Wolfe notes that RFC 36 does not allow multiple connections to share a link. He describes two cases where sharing could help: one user has several high-speed connections, or two hosts want to provide access to their separate networks over the ARPA Network.

In both cases, assigning several connections to one link could avoid a shortage of links.
sections.plainLanguage: Wolfe says one network link could carry several connections. He gives multiple high-speed transfers and links between separate networks as reasons this could be useful.

sections.title: Changes to Identify Connections
sections.content:
Wolfe proposes that the END and RDY control messages include socket numbers as well as the link number. He also says the protocol needs to clarify whether the RSM and SPD commands control an entire link or one connection.

For data messages, he proposes adding the destination socket immediately after the header. The note describes a 32-bit field for that socket.
sections.plainLanguage: Control messages would identify the socket as well as the link. Data messages would also name the destination socket so the receiver can identify the connection.

sections.title: A Future Option
sections.content: The RFC says that multiplexing itself does not need to be added immediately. Instead, Wolfe recommends changing the protocol so that multiplexing can be used later.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal is to make future link sharing possible without requiring it in the initial protocol.
